title: Radiation decontamination (cleaning off fallout)
summary: Fallout or radioactive dust on someone: save a life first, then take off the outer layer of clothes and shoes and bag them, wash gently with soap and water (no conditioner, no scrubbing) or wipe off, put on clean clothes, then help others and pets.

steps.text: Is anyone badly hurt: heavy bleeding, not breathing normally, unresponsive, or in shock?
steps.detail: Serious injuries come before cleaning off. FEMA: "Regardless of location, management of serious injury takes precedence over radiological decontamination", and "any immediate lifesaving procedures should be performed before decontamination" (FEMA planning guidance). New York State Department of Health: "Patient with life-threatening condition: treat, then decontaminate."

ask.q: Is anyone badly hurt: heavy bleeding, not breathing normally, unresponsive, or in shock?

steps.text: Take off the outer layer of clothes and shoes slowly and carefully, so the dust does not shake loose. Do it before coming in, or just inside the door, away from others.
steps.detail:
Taking off the outer layer of clothing can remove up to 90% of the radioactive material (CDC, Ready.gov, FEMA). Be very careful taking clothes off, so radioactive dust does not shake loose and get breathed in (CDC, Ready.gov). FEMA's instructions include shoes: "Remove contaminated clothes and shoes and place them in a bag" (FEMA planning guidance).

Where: CDC says to take the outer layer off before you go inside, if you can (CDC, What to Do: Get Inside). FEMA's messages say people coming in can remove shoes and outer clothing, or brush or wipe off fallout particles, immediately after they enter (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath). Either way, keep it away from other people and pets.

Try to avoid spreading the dust to parts of the body that were covered by clothes (CDC). Avoid touching your eyes, nose and mouth if you can (Ready.gov).
steps.warn: Do not shake the clothes out.

steps.text: Put the clothes and shoes in a plastic bag or other sealable container, close it, and put it out of the way, far from people and pets.
steps.detail:
CDC: put the clothing in a plastic bag or other sealable container and put the bag far away from other people and pets. If you have no bag, leave the clothes in an out-of-the-way place such as the corner of a room, and keep people away from it (CDC, Radiation Emergencies and Children). Red Cross: seal or tie the bag.

Keep cuts and scrapes covered when you handle contaminated items (CDC).

steps.text: Wash gently with soap and water: a warm (not hot) shower if you can, hair washed with shampoo or soap, no conditioner. No shower: wash uncovered skin at a sink, or wipe it.
steps.detail:
Shower (CDC): take a warm shower and gently wash yourself with lots of soap; do not scald, scrub, or scratch your skin; wash your hair with shampoo or soap. "Do not use conditioner because it will cause radioactive material to stick to your hair" (CDC; Red Cross and FEMA say the same). FEMA: try to direct the rinse water away from the face and body, and keep the material out of the eyes, nose, mouth and wounds (FEMA planning guidance).

No shower (CDC): at a sink or faucet, wash your hands, face and parts of your body that were not covered, with soap and plenty of water. No sink: use a moist wipe, a clean wet cloth or a damp paper towel, and pay special attention to the hands and face (CDC). Ready.gov: if you cannot wash, wipe any skin or hair that was not covered.

Keep cuts and scrapes covered while washing, to stop radioactive material getting into the wound (CDC, FEMA).

Showering and changing all your clothes is the best way, but you can still remove most of the radioactive material without water or a change of clothes (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath). Tap water can be used for washing even if officials say not to drink it (CDC). When water is scarce, wet wipes or other methods without water can be used (FEMA planning guidance).

Ready.gov: do not use household cleaning wipes on your skin. Hand sanitizer does not protect against radioactive material (Ready.gov).
steps.warn: No conditioner. Do not scald, scrub or scratch the skin. Keep cuts covered. No household cleaning wipes on skin.

steps.text: Gently blow the nose, and wipe the eyelids, eyelashes and ears with a clean wet cloth or moist wipe. Bag every wipe, cloth and towel you used.
steps.detail:
CDC, Red Cross, FEMA: gently blow your nose and wipe your eyelids, eyelashes and ears with a moist wipe, clean wet cloth or damp paper towel. Put used wipes, cloths and towels in a plastic bag or sealable container, away from people and pets (CDC, Ready.gov, FEMA).

Dust or grit in an eye: do not rub it; use the Eye injury protocol (rinse it out with clean water).

steps.text: Put on clean clothes from a closet, drawer or other covered place. None? Take the outer layer off, brush it off away from others with nose and mouth covered, put it back on, rewash.
steps.detail:
Clothes stored in a closet or drawer, away from the radioactive material, can be worn (CDC). They are much less likely to have radioactive material on them (FEMA).

No clean clothes (CDC): take off your outer layer of clothing, shake or brush off your clothes, and put your clothes back on; then rewash your hands, face and exposed skin at a sink or faucet. FEMA: if you cannot take off your clothes or you are only wearing one layer, brush or wipe off your clothing as best you can away from other people or pets, and cover your nose and mouth with a cloth or mask if you can, so you don't swallow any particles you shake loose (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath).

steps.text: Wounds: once the skin around a wound is clean, care for it with the Wound cleaning and care protocol. Burns: use the Burns protocol. Then help others (next).
steps.detail:
FEMA: if you're wounded, apply pressure to stop any bleeding, then decontaminate the area around the wound, and wrap physical injuries or lightly wrap burn injuries. If you are injured and need to self-decontaminate, clean around the wound, and then treat your injury as you would an ordinary injury. It is important to treat your physical injuries: apply the appropriate treatments, even if there is concern that it might result in some radiation contamination. Get a health care professional to decontaminate your wound once you have access to one (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath).

So: clean around the wound, then rinse and dress it as the Wound cleaning and care protocol says, as for any wound; a health care professional should still decontaminate the wound once one can be reached (FEMA). Burns: use the Burns protocol. What more to do if no professional can ever be reached is an open question (see the open question).

A burn that appears hours or days later on skin that was not near heat can be a radiation burn: use the Radiation sickness protocol.

steps.text: Help others who cannot clean off on their own: babies and children, older people, and anyone with a disability. Clean yourself first.
steps.detail:
FEMA: after decontaminating yourself, help others who might not be able to self-decontaminate on their own, such as babies and children, people with disabilities, people with access or functional needs, older adults, or pets (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath). CDC: if you have infants, small children or others who may need help washing, wash yourself first.

Use the same steps for them: outer clothes and shoes off and bagged, gentle washing with soap and water or wiping, no conditioner, cuts covered, clean clothes.

Let people in from outside. FEMA: allowing others to come inside with you can save their lives; "The particles are dangerous, but the people themselves are not." CDC: providing shelter to someone who was outside can save their life without endangering your own. Have them take off shoes and outer clothing before they come in if they can, then shower or wipe off at a sink (FEMA).

Children are more likely than adults to develop health effects from radiation (CDC).

Breastfeeding: CDC says nursing mothers can pass radioactive material to their babies through breastmilk, and that they should consider not breastfeeding if other milk sources are available until they can see their healthcare professional. Pregnant women should take extra precautions (CDC, Radiation Emergencies and Children). Off-grid there may be no other milk and no professional (see the open question). CDC's Infant Feeding and Frequently Asked Questions pages say it differently; all three are in Water and food after fallout (Survival), including: if you were indoors with the doors and windows closed, keep breastfeeding (CDC).

steps.text: Protect yourself while you help: waterproof gloves, a mask or cloth over nose and mouth, and something over your clothes if you have it. Keep cuts covered.
steps.detail:
FEMA: if available, put on something to cover your clothing; wear waterproof gloves and a mask (or other material to cover your nose and mouth) if you can; cover cuts and scrapes (yours and those of anyone you are helping) when washing, to keep radioactive material out of the wound (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath; CDC says the same).

Caring for someone is unlikely to be a danger to you: externally exposed patients do not become radioactive, and a person who has been exposed to radiation is unlikely to pose a radiological health risk to any other person (New York State Department of Health). CDC adds that a person with radioactive material inside the body can expose people near them to radiation from it, and that body fluids such as blood, sweat and urine can carry it; keep from touching dust and body fluids (CDC, What Causes Contamination versus Exposure).

steps.text: After helping, clean yourself again: wash your hands, face and uncovered skin.
steps.detail: FEMA: after helping others, decontaminate yourself again to make sure no radioactive materials are on you from the person or animals you helped. CDC: rewash your hands, face and exposed skin at a sink or faucet.

steps.text: Pets that were outside: wash them with shampoo or soap and water and rinse well, or brush or wipe them with a wet cloth. Wear gloves and a mask if you can. Then wash your hands and face.
steps.detail:
CDC and FEMA: wash your pet carefully (thoroughly) with shampoo or soap and water and rinse completely. If you cannot wash your pet, brush or wipe it with a wet cloth or paper towel (FEMA). Ready.gov: gently brush your pet's coat to remove radioactive particles, and wash it with soap and water if available.

Wear waterproof gloves and, if possible, a mask (CDC, FEMA). Some pets shake themselves off, so be careful of contamination (FEMA). Cover cuts on you and your pet (CDC, FEMA). Wash your hands and face afterwards (CDC). Do not touch soiled material with your bare hands (CDC). Do not shave a pet's fur instead of washing it: shaving does not get rid of fallout particles (NYC Health).

Contaminated animals that are not cleaned off can contaminate people or objects (FEMA); FEMA's planning guidance names children who pet them. Keep pets indoors (FEMA).

steps.text: Wipe the things you need, such as wallets, jewellery, wheelchairs or hearing aids, as you would wipe off dirt. Bag anything you cannot clean and do not need now, away from people and pets.
steps.detail:
FEMA: after you are inside and have self-decontaminated, you can decontaminate essential belongings such as wallets, jewelry, or assistive medical devices such as wheelchairs, prosthetic limbs or hearing aids, the same way you would remove dirt or sand. Use a damp cloth or towel or wet wipe and wear waterproof gloves. If an item cannot be decontaminated and you don't immediately need it, put it in a bag, away from people and pets; wait for further instructions from officials (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath).

Officials will tell you if the home itself needs cleaning (CDC; see Living in a closed-up house in Survival).

steps.text: Watch everyone who was outside for signs of radiation sickness: nausea, vomiting, headache, diarrhoea, or a burn on skin that was not near heat. If they appear, use the Radiation sickness protocol.
steps.detail:
Symptoms of radiation sickness include nausea, vomiting, headache and diarrhoea; they can start within minutes to days and may come and go (CDC). Radiation burns appear a few hours to several days after exposure (FEMA).

Stress causes the same symptoms in many people who were not exposed (FEMA). Being cleaned off changes nothing about the danger outside. How long to stay in, and when leaving shelter makes sense, are in the Survival topics How long to stay in and Leaving and moving after fallout.

steps.text: Treat the life threat first, with its own protocol: Severe bleeding, CPR, adult (or child or infant), Recovery position or Shock. Clean them off afterwards.
steps.detail:
Do not delay treatment for fear of becoming contaminated: externally exposed patients do not become radioactive (New York State Department of Health). FEMA: in instances of life-threatening or serious injuries, medical care takes priority over contamination screening and decontamination (FEMA planning guidance).

For a bleeding wound, FEMA's public message: apply pressure to stop any bleeding, then decontaminate the area around the wound. FEMA: it is important to treat your physical injuries; apply the appropriate treatments, even if there is concern that it might result in some radiation contamination (FEMA, Communicating in the Immediate Aftermath).

If you can do it without delaying care, wear gloves and cover your nose and mouth (FEMA), and take off the casualty's outer clothing, which removes most of the material (CDC, FEMA).

Come back to this protocol from "Take off the outer layer of clothes" once the urgent care is done. During a fallout warning, getting medical care means leaving shelter. From Leaving and moving after fallout (Survival): “Leave only if an immediate danger such as a fire, gas leak, building collapse or serious injury forces you out, or officials tell you to (Ready.gov).” Whether and how to go is in Leaving and moving after fallout (Survival).

donts: Do not delay life-saving care to clean someone off (FEMA, New York State Department of Health).
Do not shake out contaminated clothes or shoes near people or pets, or bring them into the living space unbagged (CDC, FEMA).
Do not use hair conditioner: it makes radioactive material stick to the hair (CDC, Red Cross).
Do not scald, scrub or scratch the skin (CDC, FEMA).
Do not use household cleaning wipes on skin, and do not rely on hand sanitizer: it does not protect against radioactive material (Ready.gov).
Do not let the dust get into cuts, eyes, nose or mouth: keep cuts covered while washing (CDC, FEMA).
Do not forget to clean yourself again after helping someone else or a pet (FEMA, CDC).
evacuate: This list says what needs medical care. During a fallout warning, whether and when to leave shelter to reach it is covered in Leaving and moving after fallout (Survival).
Needs medical care: any serious, life-threatening injury (FEMA).

Needs medical care: signs of radiation sickness after being near the explosion or out in fallout, or a burn on skin that was not near heat, a chemical or electricity (FEMA, CDC). See the Radiation sickness protocol.
Needs medical care: the wound problems listed in the Wound cleaning and care protocol, and the burns listed in the Burns protocol.
